description: The service may fail to manage uploaded videos in a compliant way, for example by lacking a lawful basis, collecting more data than necessary for approval/rejection, retaining uploads too long, or mishandling children's personal data contained in the videos.
assumptions: Uploaded videos can contain personal data of children and other individuals, triggering heightened compliance obligations.

title: Insufficient evidence about upload submission and moderation outcome
description: If the service does not maintain appropriate privacy-respecting records of the upload, approval/rejection decision, and related notices, the parent may be unable to prove what was submitted or how it was handled, while the service may also be unable to demonstrate accountable processing.
assumptions: The workflow includes moderation decisions and possible disputes about whether a video was uploaded, reviewed, approved, rejected, or deleted.
uncertainty_note: Exact Nr subtree node is approximate; included because approval/rejection workflows commonly create repudiation disputes.

title: Streaming reveals the child's viewing activity to the service
description: By sending the approved video stream, the Video Management Service necessarily learns and can expose that the child user is watching a specific approved video at a specific time. This creates detectability of the child's consumption activity beyond what is strictly needed for delivery if such events are logged, monitored, or correlated.
assumptions: The service can observe or record stream start/stop events, video identifiers, timestamps, and recipient identifiers as part of delivery.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen by best judgement; retrieved context did not include the detailed D threat tree for this flow.

title: Stream metadata can link the child to specific content consumption
description: Metadata on the streaming flow, such as session identifiers, IP address, device identifiers, timing, and requested video identifiers, may allow an observer or intermediary to link multiple viewing sessions to the same child or household and build a profile of viewing habits.
assumptions: The flow carries observable metadata even if payload content is encrypted; network or platform intermediaries may access some of it.
uncertainty_note: Exact L threat-tree node may differ depending on the project's tree version; node selected by best judgement.

title: Stream or metadata may identify the child or household in transit
description: Identifiers in the stream delivery path, including account-linked tokens, persistent device identifiers, or network metadata, may enable identification of the child user or their household by parties observing the transmission.
assumptions: Delivery uses identifiers or tokens that are stable enough to be associated with a specific child account, device, or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact I node selected by best judgement because detailed threat-tree excerpts were not provided.

title: Video playback on the child's device may be observable by others nearby
description: Once the stream reaches the child user, the act of receiving and playing the approved video may make the child's viewing activity detectable to parents, siblings, peers, or others with access to the device or surroundings, revealing interests or habits.
assumptions: The child consumes the stream on a shared or observable device/environment.
uncertainty_note: Included as a destination-side privacy threat only if local observability of playback is in scope for the model.

title: Streaming and associated telemetry may exceed compliant data minimization or retention limits
description: Delivering the video may involve collection or retention of playback telemetry, identifiers, and engagement data about a child. If the service shares more data than necessary for streaming, or retains viewing records longer than permitted, the flow contributes to non-compliant personal data management.
assumptions: The service logs or stores streaming-related personal data about a child user, and child-specific legal or policy obligations apply.
uncertainty_note: Nc.2 is supported by retrieved context; applicability depends on whether telemetry/logging accompanies this flow.

title: Excessive disclosure of child browsing data from profiles store
description: The childprofiles collection may disclose more personal data to the AI Recommendation Engine than is strictly necessary for generating recommendations. Because the data concerns children's browsing behavior, over-sharing from the datastore increases privacy risk and may violate data minimization expectations.
assumptions: Assumes the planned transfer includes raw or broad browsing-history fields rather than a narrowly scoped feature set required for recommendation generation.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimization structure; exact subnode may differ in the canonical tree.

title: AI engine can link child browsing records across sessions or profiles
description: On receipt of browsing data, the AI Recommendation Engine may combine records over time or with other inputs to build persistent child-level profiles. This enables linkage of events and attributes that were previously separate, increasing the ability to track a child across sessions, contexts, or devices.
assumptions: Assumes P4 stores identifiers, stable pseudonyms, device/account signals, or model features that permit correlation over time.
uncertainty_note: Exact LINDDUN Pro subnode may vary; linkage at the destination is strongly applicable even if the precise node id is approximate.

title: AI engine may identify a child from browsing data or correlated signals
description: Browsing data sent to the AI engine may contain direct identifiers or sufficiently unique behavioral patterns that allow the engine to identify an individual child, especially when combined with account, device, or household context already available to the engine.
assumptions: Assumes P4 has access to auxiliary data or receives quasi-identifiers alongside browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Identification risk is genuine for behavioral data, but the exact subnode id is approximate.

title: AI engine can infer sensitive traits from child browsing behavior
description: Processing child browsing data for recommendations can reveal or derive sensitive interests, vulnerabilities, developmental traits, health-related concerns, religious views, or other intimate characteristics that were not explicitly provided. Such inference increases privacy impact beyond the original data collected.
assumptions: Assumes recommendation models derive latent features, segments, or predictions from browsing behavior.
uncertainty_note: Destination-side detectability/inference threat is clear, though the exact tree-node id is best-effort.

title: Use of child browsing data for recommendations may be insufficiently transparent
description: Children or their guardians may not understand that browsing data stored in childprofiles is being repurposed by an AI engine to generate recommendations, profile behavior, or derive interests. The planned nature of the flow suggests a risk that this downstream use is not made adequately visible or understandable.
assumptions: Assumes notices, explanations, or age-appropriate transparency mechanisms do not clearly describe this AI use.
uncertainty_note: Unawareness is plausible from the flow description, but depends on the system's notice and explanation design.

title: AI recommendation use may exceed the consent or legal basis for children's data
description: If child browsing data was originally collected for service operation or history storage, sending it to the AI Recommendation Engine for personalization may go beyond the consent, parental authorization, or other legal basis originally obtained. This creates a non-compliance risk, especially given heightened protections for children's data.
assumptions: Assumes the existing consent/legal basis does not explicitly cover AI-driven personalization or profiling of children's browsing behavior.
uncertainty_note: Strong privacy/compliance concern, but applicability depends on the actual consent text, parental controls, and jurisdiction.

title: Unnecessary disclosure of browsing data to third-party advertisers
description: The AI Recommendation Engine plans to send users' browsing data to third-party advertisers. Browsing data is personal data and sharing it with advertisers is a disclosure across a system boundary. If this sharing is not strictly necessary for the service requested by the user, it violates data minimization and creates an avoidable explicit data disclosure threat.
assumptions: Browsing data contains personal or behaviorally identifying information and the advertising purpose is not strictly necessary to deliver the core recommendation service.
uncertainty_note: Tree node selection is based on best judgement for explicit/intentional third-party disclosure; exact sub-node label may vary by LINDDUN Pro tree version.

title: Secondary use or over-processing of received browsing data by advertisers
description: Once third-party advertisers receive the browsing data, they may retain, enrich, profile, or reuse it for purposes beyond the original sharing context, causing further avoidable disclosure of personal information and expansion of who can learn sensitive behavioral patterns.
assumptions: Advertisers are separate controllers/processors and may combine received browsing data with their own datasets for ad targeting, profiling, or onward sharing.
uncertainty_note: Exact Dd sub-node is approximate; the core issue is destination-side disclosure/over-processing by the third party.

title: Sharing browsing data with advertisers may occur without valid user consent or another appropriate legal basis
description: Planned transmission of browsing data to third-party advertisers is likely subject to consent or another specific legal basis. If the recommendation engine shares the data without obtaining and honoring valid permission, or without providing adequate notice and choice, the flow is non-compliant with privacy requirements.
assumptions: Applicable law or policy requires consent, opt-in, or another clearly documented legal basis for third-party advertising use of browsing data.
uncertainty_note: Legal basis depends on jurisdiction and implementation details, but advertising disclosures commonly require strong consent/compliance controls.

title: Advertisers can link browsing data to existing advertising profiles
description: Third-party advertisers commonly possess identifiers, cookies, device fingerprints, or account-level data. Receiving browsing data from the recommendation engine may allow them to link this flow to existing profiles, correlating activity across services and contexts.
assumptions: The shared browsing data includes direct identifiers, persistent identifiers, or sufficiently distinctive behavioral attributes.
uncertainty_note: Exact L sub-node is approximate; the threat clearly concerns destination-side linkability through profile enrichment.

title: Advertisers may identify users from shared browsing data
description: Even if the browsing data is not overtly labeled with a real name, advertisers may use identifiers or auxiliary datasets to single out and identify the individual behind the browsing behavior.
assumptions: Advertisers have access to auxiliary data such as cookie graphs, device identifiers, account data, or brokered datasets.
uncertainty_note: Sub-node is selected by best judgement; identifiability depends on the exact fields shared and the advertiser's auxiliary data.

title: Browsing data may reveal sensitive interests or attributes to advertisers
description: Browsing histories and interaction patterns can expose interests, habits, health concerns, political views, religion, sexuality, or other sensitive characteristics. By receiving this data, advertisers may infer or directly learn private facts about users.
assumptions: Browsing data includes URLs, page categories, search/referral context, timestamps, or other signals from which sensitive topics can be inferred.
uncertainty_note: Exact D sub-node is approximate; the threat is destination-side detectability/discoverability of sensitive personal facts from browsing behavior.

title: Data in transit may expose stable identifiers enabling cross-context linkage
description: During transmission to advertisers, the flow may contain stable identifiers or metadata such as cookie IDs, device IDs, account IDs, or request metadata. These data elements enable the advertiser to correlate this transfer with other observations and datasets, increasing linkability across contexts.
assumptions: The transmitted payload or protocol metadata includes persistent identifiers or distinctive combinations of attributes.
uncertainty_note: This is a flow-centric linkability threat focused on the content/metadata of the transmission rather than interception by an attacker.

title: Collection and storage of excessive identity-document data
description: The authentication service stores full government ID images in the file system. Full images typically contain more personal data than is strictly necessary for many authentication or verification purposes, creating an avoidable disclosure through over-collection and persistence of highly sensitive identity data.
assumptions: Assumes the service could achieve its purpose with less data than full image retention, such as extracted attributes, redacted images, or short-lived processing.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on LINDDUN Pro data-disclosure/minimality concepts; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Unnecessary retention of government ID images in backend file storage
description: On receipt, the file system stores government ID images, which may persist longer than necessary for the authentication purpose. Retaining raw ID images increases exposure of sensitive personal data and constitutes avoidable disclosure if no strict retention limit or deletion policy is enforced.
assumptions: Assumes DS4 is persistent storage and that retention/deletion controls are not guaranteed by the model.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree subnode is approximate; the core issue is destination-side avoidable disclosure via storage/retention.

title: Government ID images enable direct identification of the user
description: The destination stores raw government ID images, which inherently contain strong identifiers such as name, photo, document number, date of birth, and address. This makes the data directly identifying at rest and raises identifiability risk if the storage is accessed or reused beyond the immediate verification purpose.
uncertainty_note: Identifiability clearly applies, but the exact subnode id is a best-effort selection.

title: Stored ID images can be linked across sessions or services
description: Persisting government ID images in a backend file system enables records relating to the same individual to be linked across authentication attempts, accounts, or other datasets using stable document attributes or the image itself. This creates a linkability risk beyond what is necessary for a single verification event.
assumptions: Assumes stored files or associated metadata can be correlated over time or with other records.
uncertainty_note: Exact subnode id is approximate; applicability depends on whether DS4 supports correlation with other records.

title: Storage of ID images may exceed user expectations or stated purpose
description: Users may provide government ID images expecting one-time identity verification, while backend file-system storage can imply broader processing, persistence, or secondary use. If this storage is not transparent, specific, and aligned with the communicated purpose, it creates a non-compliance risk with purpose limitation, transparency, and data-minimization obligations.
assumptions: Assumes the model does not demonstrate explicit notice, consent where applicable, or a clearly bounded legal basis and retention policy for storing raw ID images.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance depends on the actual notice/legal basis/retention controls, which are not shown in the DFD.

title: JWT in localStorage can identify the user on this browser
description: Storing a JWT in browser localStorage makes the token persistently available to scripts running in the origin. If the JWT contains subject, account, tenant, or other unique claims, the stored value can directly identify the user or single them out on this device/browser.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT contains stable user-related claims or otherwise functions as a unique bearer identifier for the session/account.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort based on general LINDDUN identification semantics; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Persistent JWT storage enables linkability across sessions and actions
description: A JWT stored in localStorage is typically persistent across page reloads and browser restarts until explicitly cleared. The same token or stable claims within it can be reused to correlate multiple visits, requests, or user actions within the same origin, linking events that might otherwise remain less connected.
assumptions: Assumes the token lifetime is longer than a single transient interaction and that the JWT value or embedded claims remain stable enough to correlate events.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree sub-node is approximate; applicability is strong even if the precise node label differs.

title: JWT contents in localStorage may disclose personal data
description: JWTs often contain readable claims such as user ID, email, roles, tenant, or other attributes. When stored in localStorage, these claims are accessible to any script executing in the origin and to anyone with local browser access, increasing the risk of disclosure of personal data beyond what is necessary for authentication.
assumptions: Assumes the JWT is not encrypted and carries personal or account-related claims, as is common for JWT access or ID tokens.
uncertainty_note: If the JWT is opaque or contains no personal claims, disclosure impact would be lower.

title: Users may be unaware that authentication tokens persist in localStorage
description: Storing the JWT in localStorage can create a hidden persistence mechanism: users may believe closing the tab or browser ends authentication, while the token remains stored and usable. This can undermine user awareness of how long authentication state persists on the device.
assumptions: Assumes the application does not clearly communicate token persistence or provide obvious controls to clear it.
uncertainty_note: This is context-dependent on the application's UX and notices.

title: Persistent token storage may exceed user expectations or consent
description: Persisting a JWT in localStorage can retain authentication state and associated identifiers on the device longer than users expect, especially on shared devices. If this persistence is not necessary, clearly disclosed, or configurable, the storage practice may not align with consent, choice, or data-minimization expectations.
assumptions: Assumes token persistence is not strictly necessary for the service or is not transparently communicated to the user.
uncertainty_note: Whether this is a true non-compliance issue depends on the system's legal basis, notices, retention policy, and jurisdiction.

title: Excessive disclosure of child history to parent
description: The process may disclose more of the child's history than is necessary for the parent's review purpose, such as detailed events, sensitive notes, or historical records beyond the relevant scope. This creates a privacy risk because the act of sharing from P3 exposes potentially sensitive child data to the parent.
assumptions: Assumes the child history can contain sensitive or granular records and that not all retrieved history is strictly necessary for the parent's immediate review task.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general LINDDUN disclosure categorization; exact subnode may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Further disclosure or onward sharing by parent recipient
description: Once the child history is received, the parent user may store, copy, screenshot, or share the information onward beyond the intended context. The privacy threat arises at the destination because the recipient's handling can expand disclosure of the child's personal data.
assumptions: Assumes the parent interface allows viewing or exporting information in a way that can be retained or reshared outside the system.
uncertainty_note: Exact threat-tree subnode may differ depending on whether the catalog distinguishes internal receipt from onward transfer.

title: Insufficient transparency about what child history is shown to the parent
description: The process may provide child history to the parent without making it clear to the child or parent what categories of history are included, why they are included, and under what rules access is granted. This can undermine users' understanding of the data use.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not clearly explain the scope and rationale of parent-visible child history.
uncertainty_note: Applies if transparency notices or contextual explanations are absent or weak.

title: Sharing child history without valid consent or appropriate legal basis
description: Providing the child's history to the parent may be non-compliant if the system lacks a valid legal basis, does not respect age-dependent rights of the child, or fails to enforce consent/authorization rules for parental access. The privacy threat arises from the source process deciding to share the data.
assumptions: Assumes parental access may be restricted by jurisdiction, custody status, age of the child, or specific consent settings.
uncertainty_note: This depends strongly on legal context and business rules for parental rights and child autonomy.

title: Identification of child or parent through data in transit
description: The transmitted child history or associated metadata may directly identify the child or parent, or make them identifiable when intercepted or observed in transit. Even if the content is intended for the parent, identifiers and contextual details on the flow can reveal who the data concerns.
assumptions: Assumes the flow carries names, account identifiers, timestamps, relationship indicators, or other identifying attributes.
uncertainty_note: Primarily relevant if transport protections, endpoint exposure, or observable metadata are insufficient.

title: Linking child history with parent identity via flow metadata
description: Metadata and content on the flow can link a specific child profile and historical records to a specific parent account. This association may enable broader profiling of the child-parent relationship or correlation with other datasets.
assumptions: Assumes recurring identifiers, account references, or stable relationship markers are present on the flow or inferable from it.
uncertainty_note: Linking is inherent to the function; the threat applies where that linkage could be used beyond the intended review purpose.

title: Parent can plausibly deny having accessed the child's history
description: If the system does not provide adequate evidence of access, the parent may later deny having viewed sensitive child history. This weakens accountability for privacy-relevant access to the child's data.
assumptions: Assumes access logging, receipts, or audit trails for parent viewing are absent or insufficient.
uncertainty_note: Non-repudiation is included in LINDDUN, but exact applicability depends on whether accountability for access is a privacy requirement in this system.
